title: Travelling salesman: permutation enumeration vs Held-Karp DP
problem_statement: Given an n x n matrix of non-negative integer distances, compute the minimum total length of a tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the start.

algorithms.name: permutation enumeration
algorithms.idea: Fix city 0 as the start and evaluate all (n-1)! orders of the remaining cities.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each permutation p of 1..n-1: best = min(best, length(0, p, 0))

algorithms.name: Held-Karp dynamic programming
algorithms.idea: best[S][j] = shortest path from city 0 through exactly the set S, ending at j. Combine over subsets of increasing size.
algorithms.correctness: Held & Karp 1962; Bellman 1962: optimal substructure over (visited set, last city).

relationship: Factorial -> single exponential: n! vs n^2 2^n. A real, large improvement that still stays exponential. No polynomial algorithm is known; TSP is NP-hard, so one would imply P = NP.

sources.title: A dynamic programming approach to sequencing problems
sources.venue: Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics 10(1), 196-210

sources.title: Dynamic programming treatment of the travelling salesman problem
Reducibility among combinatorial problems
sources.venue: Complexity of Computer Computations, Plenum Press, 85-103
sources.note: NP-completeness of Hamiltonian cycle, hence NP-hardness of TSP.

verification.method: V1: both agree on random asymmetric distance matrices (weights 1..100, n <= 8 for enumeration) and respect independent bounds. V2: runtimes fitted against n! and n^2 2^n.

caveats: Primary T6 because polynomial time is open (NP-hard); secondary T8 for the verified factorial -> single-exponential improvement.
notes: Shows that dramatic speedups (factorial -> 2^n) can exist while the polynomial barrier is untouched.
